why: This file is two jobs stapled together, and only one of them is bespoke. Job one -- fetch the OpenRouter catalogue, keep the zero-priced entries, cache it for a day, pick a model, and fail over to a sibling when one returns 429 (client.py:101-255) -- is commodity in 2026 and at least two named alternatives cover most of it: simonw/llm-openrouter already ships model listing with a --free filter and a cache-refresh command, and OpenRouter itself now publishes an `openrouter/free` router slug whose own page (fetched 2026-07-29) says it 'selects free models at random from the models available on OpenRouter' and 'smartly filters for models that support features needed for your request' across '17 Models in this router' -- that is server-side, zero-code, zero-dependency failover that would delete pick_model, candidates, PREFERRED and most of chat's retry loop, roughly 80 lines by my count from reading. Job two has no off-the-shelf equivalent I could find: a PRE-FLIGHT local ceiling that refuses to send the 51st request of the UTC day and sleeps 3s between calls before the request leaves (client.py:207-217 via tools/lib/quota.py:77-96), where a 429 is logged but explicitly NOT counted against the allowance (client.py:227-233), plus a refute mode whose exit code IS the verdict -- 0 supported, 1 refuted, 2 unparseable, 3 quota exhausted (client.py:330-334, 455-457) -- so a shell gate can branch on it. LiteLLM has the closest thing to the first property and it is a Proxy feature: its own docs for user/team/key budgets and rpm_limit state 'Need to a postgres database', which is a server plus a database to replace 121 lines of stdlib JSONL for a single-maintainer offline repo. So: adopt for the routing half, keep ours for the ledger and the exit-code contract, and stop describing the failover loop as something that had to be written.

alternatives.name: OpenRouter's own `openrouter/free` router slug (openrouter.ai/openrouter/free)
alternatives.covers: the entire failover-across-zero-priced-models responsibility, server-side and for free. Its model page (fetched 2026-07-29) states it is 'a router that selects free models at random from the models available on OpenRouter' and 'smartly filters for models that support features needed for your request', currently '17 Models in this router'. Passing it as --model would make pick_model (client.py:133-141), candidates (client.py:174-187), PREFERRED (client.py:67) and the retry loop in chat (client.py:215-255) dead code -- roughly 80 lines, estimated by reading, not by doing the edit.
alternatives.gap: selects at random, so it cannot honour a stated preference order, and two runs of the same refutation can land on different weights with no way to pin the first choice. It returns one final model id, not the per-attempt {model, status, error} trail that chat() returns as `tried` and cmd_refute prints as `failed_over_from` (client.py:239-245, 327-328) -- provenance the docstring calls load-bearing because 'a silent substitution would make a refutation impossible to reproduce'. It also enforces nothing locally: the 50/day and 20/min ceilings are still discovered as a 429 rather than prevented, which is the exact failure tools/lib/quota.py:1-19 exists to stop. I did NOT verify that `openrouter/free` is itself billed at zero in /api/v1/models, nor which rate-limit bucket it draws from, nor whether its 'feature filtering' excludes the audio and safety-classifier models that _text_capable (client.py:153-171) exists to exclude.
alternatives.cost: zero install, zero dependencies, one string change. Adds a dependency on one vendor product feature that can be renamed or withdrawn -- the same class of breakage the module docstring already names for individual free slugs (client.py:18-21).
alternatives.maturity: the page is live and rendered a model count on 2026-07-29. I did not find a changelog, deprecation policy, or SLA for the router, and did not call it.

alternatives.name: simonw/llm + simonw/llm-openrouter plugin (github.com/simonw/llm-openrouter)
alternatives.covers: close to all of the non-refute CLI surface. Its README (fetched 2026-07-29) documents `llm openrouter models` with '--free for a list of just the models that are available for free' and a --json output, an `llm openrouter key` subcommand that prints the key's rate_limit block, and per the 0.6 release notes 'a command for refreshing the list of available models without waiting for the cache to expire' -- that is cmd_models, cmd_key, catalogue caching and --refresh (client.py:101-116, 347-372) already built and maintained by someone else. The parent `llm` tool also logs every prompt and response to SQLite, covering the audit half of the ledger.
alternatives.gap: asked directly whether it enforces a local daily quota or paces requests before sending, the README yields nothing: it displays OpenRouter's advertised rate_limit but does not gate on it, so there is no equivalent of quota.guard() refusing call 51 or quota.pace() sleeping 3s (client.py:216-217). No documented automatic fallback on 429/503 -- the README has no retry or fallback section at all. `llm` logs, but logging is not enforcement, and its SQLite log has no notion of 'this 429 does not count against today' (client.py:227-228). And nothing in it produces the refute contract: adversarial system prompt, fenced-JSON extraction, and exit 1 on refuted (client.py:258-334) would be a wrapper you write anyway.
alternatives.cost: two pip installs (llm, then llm install llm-openrouter) plus their dependency trees, into a tool that today imports only stdlib plus two sibling files in this repo. Apache-2.0 per the project; I did not open the LICENSE file to confirm.
alternatives.maturity: GitHub releases page lists 0.1 through 0.6 with 0.6 the newest. The dates WebFetch returned were internally inconsistent (it placed 0.4.1 before 0.4), so I do NOT trust the specific dates and did not verify current maintenance cadence, open-issue count, or whether it tracks OpenRouter API changes promptly. I also did not read llm_openrouter.py, so whether --free filters on the pricing fields (as free_models does at client.py:126-130) or merely on the ':free' slug suffix is unverified -- that distinction is the difference between a price guarantee and a naming convention.

alternatives.name: LiteLLM (BerriAI, docs.litellm.ai) -- SDK and Proxy
alternatives.covers: the widest overlap of anything found. The SDK gives one OpenAI-shaped call across 100+ providers with built-in retry and client-side fallbacks, which is chat()'s failover with far more edge-case handling than a single try/except around urllib (client.py:80-94). The Proxy adds max_budget, rpm_limit, tpm_limit and max_parallel_requests per key/user/team -- conceptually the closest published thing to this component's daily ceiling.
alternatives.gap: the budget and rate-limit half is Proxy-only. Its own users/budgets doc (fetched 2026-07-29) states the requirement plainly -- 'Need to a postgres database (e.g. Supabase, Neon, etc)' -- and documents no standalone-SDK equivalent, so adopting the property this component actually cares about means running a server plus Postgres to replace 121 lines of append-only JSONL. Its limits are also per-key spend and rpm/tpm, not 'N requests per UTC day where a 429 does not count', which is the specific accounting in quota.py:68-72 and client.py:227-228. Nothing in it filters a catalogue to strictly-zero-priced entries, nothing implements the output_modalities == ['text'] exact-match rule, and nothing produces a refute exit code.
alternatives.cost: SDK-only adoption is a large pip dependency (it reimplements provider interfaces rather than wrapping official SDKs, per the comparison writeups found) for a tool that makes exactly one endpoint call. Proxy adoption is a server process plus Postgres. Free/open-source core.
alternatives.maturity: docs are current and the project is widely covered in 2026 gateway comparisons. I did not check release cadence, did not run `gh release list`, and did not install it.

alternatives.name: OpenAI Python SDK pointed at OpenRouter (base_url='https://openrouter.ai/api/v1')
alternatives.covers: the transport. OpenRouter's quickstart confirms it 'works with the OpenAI Python SDK out of the box -- just change base_url', giving typed responses, tested retry/timeout handling, streaming and tool calling in place of the hand-rolled _http (client.py:70-94).
alternatives.gap: it hands back typed Model objects for /models; the fields this component filters on -- pricing.prompt, pricing.completion, architecture.output_modalities -- are OpenRouter extensions, not OpenAI schema, so free_models and _text_capable (client.py:126-171) would be reading untyped extra fields anyway. More importantly the SDK's exception hierarchy folds transport failure and provider rejection into different exception classes but nothing maps them onto quota accounting: _http deliberately returns status 0 for a URLError (client.py:91-94) precisely so that 'no network' lands in RETRY_STATUS and is NOT counted against the daily allowance, a three-line design the docstring justifies as 'how a dead channel gets reported as a refuted claim'. That mapping is hand-written either way. No quota, no pacing, no refute contract.
alternatives.cost: a pip dependency and its httpx/pydantic tree to replace 25 lines of urllib in a stdlib-only repo. MIT licensed.
alternatives.maturity: first-party, actively maintained. Not independently verified this session; I did not install it or check its current version.

alternatives.name: mozilla-ai/any-llm and andrewyng/aisuite (unified LLM interface libraries)
alternatives.covers: the provider-abstraction layer. any-llm reached 1.0 with a stable API surface, async-first calls and reusable clients per its release coverage; aisuite offers a lightweight unified Chat Completions API. Either would let the refute prompt be pointed at a non-OpenRouter provider without rewriting the call site.
alternatives.gap: both are interface-normalisation libraries. Neither publishes any spend ceiling, request ledger, or per-day counter -- the property this component was built for. Neither has a zero-price catalogue filter (any-llm normalises the CALL, not the model list), neither excludes audio or safety-classifier models by output modality, and neither produces a refute verdict or an exit code. Adopting one would abstract a provider this tool is deliberately pinned to for one reason -- it is the vendor whose free tier exists.
alternatives.cost: one pip dependency each. any-llm leverages official provider SDKs, so its transitive tree pulls those in too. Both open-source; I did not read either LICENSE.
alternatives.maturity: any-llm 1.0 shipped and is Mozilla.ai-backed per its blog and InfoWorld coverage; the same coverage says aisuite 'lacks active maintenance, comprehensive testing, and modern Python typing standards', which I am reporting as a sourced third-party claim, not something I verified against the repository.

alternatives.name: Zen MCP Server (beehiveinnovations/zen-mcp-server) and similar cross-LLM MCP servers
alternatives.covers: the actual stated purpose in the docstring -- 'a second opinion from a model that is not me' -- as an MCP server Claude Code connects to directly, routing subtasks to Gemini, OpenAI, Ollama and others with tools for code review, debugging and security audit, and explicitly marketed for the 'second opinion' use case with cross-model consensus. This is the product-shaped answer to why this file exists at all.
alternatives.gap: it is a tool Claude calls during a conversation, not a process that returns an exit code to a shell. The whole point of cmd_refute (client.py:291-334) is that a gate or a script can run it and branch on 0/1/2/3 without a model in the loop; an MCP tool result is text handed back to the same model whose claim is being checked, which reintroduces exactly the dependency the refutation channel is meant to break. It also has no free-tier budget enforcement, no zero-price constraint (it assumes you hold paid keys for the providers you route to), and it is a server to install and keep running.
alternatives.cost: a server process plus API keys for whichever providers you route to -- the paid-key assumption is the disqualifier for a channel whose premise is 'zero cost' (client.py:8-10).
alternatives.maturity: widely listed across MCP directories in 2026. I verified only that multiple directory listings and its README describe the multi-model second-opinion feature; I did not check the repository's commit activity, release history, or which forks are current -- the search surfaced several forks (jray2123, CrackerCat, 199-biotechnologies) which is itself a maintenance smell I did not resolve.

alternatives.name: PyrateLimiter (vutran1710/PyrateLimiter) -- for the quota half specifically
alternatives.covers: the pacing and ceiling mechanics. It is a leaky-bucket limiter supporting multiple simultaneous windows (e.g. per-minute and per-day together, which is exactly the 20/min + 50/day pair) with pluggable persistent backends including SQLite, so a limit survives process restarts. It would replace quota.guard/pace (tools/lib/quota.py:77-96) with maintained code.
alternatives.gap: it limits, it does not account. There is no notion of 'this attempt reached the provider and counts, that 429 was refused and does not' (client.py:227-228, quota.py:68-72) -- a bucket decrements on acquisition, so a throttled call would burn allowance the provider never charged. Its windows are rolling durations, not calendar days; OpenRouter resets at 00:00 UTC and quota.py:16-19 documents choosing UTC deliberately because a local-midnight reset would zero the counter while the provider still counts. And the append-only JSONL is also the audit record this repo mines later (quota.py:10-14); a limiter's bucket state is not a history. I did NOT verify PyrateLimiter's SQLite backend semantics across a UTC day boundary or whether it can express a fixed calendar-day window at all.
alternatives.cost: one pip dependency into a stdlib-only file; MIT per the project page, not verified by reading the LICENSE.
alternatives.maturity: published on PyPI with an active GitHub repo. I did not check its latest version or release date. Note the widely-circulated gist 'Every python rate-limiting library (that I can find) is broken, at least a little' surfaced in the same search -- I did not read its analysis of this specific library, so treat that as an unresolved flag, not a finding.

alternatives.name: promptfoo / DeepEval / Inspect AI (UK AISI) -- LLM-as-judge and adversarial-eval frameworks
alternatives.covers: the refute half at industrial scale: structured judge prompts, JSON-schema-constrained verdicts, graders, and CI integration. DeepEval is pytest-native and fails a build on metric thresholds, which is the same 'exit code is the verdict' shape as cmd_refute. Inspect AI ships composable scorers and 200+ prebuilt evals. promptfoo brings red-team plugins.
alternatives.gap: all three are dataset-and-suite oriented: you define cases, run a suite, get a score report. This component checks ONE ad-hoc claim, typed at a terminal or read from a file because a long claim does not survive shell quoting (client.py:292-296), and answers in under a second with an exit code. Standing up an eval framework, a config file and a case definition to ask 'is this one sentence supported' is the wrong granularity. None of them enforces a free-tier daily ceiling before dispatch, none filters a provider catalogue to zero-priced text-only models, and running them against paid models defeats the cost premise. Worth noting against ours as well: the research surfaced (arxiv 2603.28488, and the 'coin flip for safety' and AdvJudge-Zero papers) reports that LLM judges show structural negativity bias and are manipulable -- REFUTE_SYSTEM (client.py:258-273) instructs 'Default to refuted=true', which leans into that bias by design and is not calibrated against anything.
alternatives.cost: each is a framework install with config; free/open-source cores with paid SaaS tiers alongside (promptfoo, DeepEval/Confident AI). Inspect AI is open-source from UK AISI.
alternatives.maturity: all three are actively developed and heavily written about in 2026 comparison posts. I verified feature claims only from search-result summaries and one Inspect AI project page -- I did not install, run, or read the source of any of them, and I did not read the arxiv papers beyond their titles and the summarised finding.

evidence: Read in full: tools/openrouter/client.py:1-461 (the only file in the directory; __pycache__ is the sole other entry, confirmed by ls) and tools/lib/quota.py:1-121, which client.py:49 imports and which supplies the ceiling this record calls the retained property. tools/lib/envload.py was NOT read (196 lines); I took client.py:24-26 and :48 at their word that require() resolves the key case-insensitively and never prints it. quota.py and envload.py are covered by docs/prior-art/tools-lib.json (verdict keep-ours), so this record scopes to client.py's 461 lines and cites quota.py only as the mechanism behind the property claimed. Read docs/prior-art/tools-gate.json in full as the format exemplar. Grepped the repo for callers: tools/review/panel.py:554-581 sys.path-inserts this directory and calls orc.chat() for its --allow-external second opinion, so the chat() surface has a real in-repo consumer beyond the CLI. Searches run (2026-07-29): 'LiteLLM fallbacks unified LLM API OpenRouter free models budget limits'; 'simonw llm CLI plugin openrouter llm-openrouter free models'; 'python library local rate limit daily quota ledger free tier API requests per day pyrate-limiter'; 'cross-model adversarial verification LLM judge refute claim structured JSON verdict harness promptfoo deepeval inspect-ai'; 'OpenRouter official Python SDK openai-python base_url models endpoint pricing zero filter 2026'; 'MCP server second opinion another model Claude Code zen-mcp-server'; 'aisuite any-llm mozilla unified LLM python library provider fallback'. Pages fetched: openrouter.ai/openrouter/free (the router slug and its '17 Models' / random-selection wording), openrouter.ai/docs/api-reference/limits (which CONFIRMS the two constants at client.py:53-54 against the primary source as of 2026-07-29: 20 requests/minute for :free variants, 50/day under $10 lifetime credit, 1000/day at $10+ -- worth recording because a third-party 2026 blog in the same result set claimed '200/day', and the code matches the vendor doc, not the blog), github.com/simonw/llm-openrouter README, github.com/simonw/llm-openrouter releases, docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/users. NOT verified, explicitly: I ran nothing -- no client.py invocation, no API call, no quota consumed, the key was never touched; I installed and benchmarked no alternative, so every migration line count here is an estimate from reading; I did not read llm_openrouter.py's source, so its --free filter's actual predicate is unknown; I did not confirm `openrouter/free` is itself zero-priced in /api/v1/models; the llm-openrouter release dates WebFetch returned were self-contradictory and I discarded them; I did not read any of the arxiv papers surfaced; and I did not check whether the free catalogue currently contains any model matching PREFERRED (client.py:67), so the claim that the preference order still resolves is untested today.
recheck: 1) Does the router make the failover loop dead code -- run `python C:/Users/shova/claude-setup/tools/openrouter/client.py ask "reply PONG" --model openrouter/free --max-tokens 8` and, in the same session, `curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models | python -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin)['data'];r=[m for m in d if m['id']=='openrouter/free'];print(r[0]['pricing'] if r else 'ABSENT')"`. If it answers AND its pricing.prompt and pricing.completion are both '0', execute the split: delete pick_model/candidates/PREFERRED and collapse chat()'s retry loop (client.py:133-255, ~80 lines). If it is ABSENT or non-zero-priced, the vendor withdrew it and this record flips back to keep-ours. 2) Does the retained half shrink -- `gh release list --repo BerriAI/litellm --limit 5` then WebSearch 'litellm python sdk persistent daily request budget without proxy postgres'; if the plain SDK gains a durable per-day request ceiling with no server, the quota half is adoptable too. 3) `gh release list --repo simonw/llm-openrouter --limit 5` and grep its current README for 'daily', 'quota', 'fallback'; if it now enforces a local ceiling or fails over on 429, the CLI surface (cmd_models/cmd_key/catalogue, client.py:101-116 and 347-372) should be dropped in its favour. 4) Re-fetch https://openrouter.ai/docs/api-reference/limits and diff against FREE_PER_DAY=50 and MIN_INTERVAL_S=3.0 (client.py:53-54) -- if the vendor changed either number, the constants are wrong and the ceiling is either useless or blocking.
what_ours_does: client.py is a single-file CLI (six subcommands wired at client.py:414-457: ask, refute, models, key, quota, selftest) that reaches OpenRouter over stdlib urllib only. It exists because the intended external reviewer, the `codex` binary, was found not to be installed on this machine on 2026-07-25 (client.py:4-10), and the refutation premise needs weights that did not produce the claim. Money can never be spent: catalogue() fetches /api/v1/models unauthenticated and caches it 24h (client.py:101-116, with --refresh), then free_models() keeps only entries whose pricing.prompt AND pricing.completion parse to exactly 0.0 (client.py:119-130) -- a price test on live data, not a trust of the ':free' slug convention, which matters because the docstring records that free slugs churn weekly and a stale hardcoded id fails as a 404 that reads like an auth error (client.py:18-21). _text_capable() (client.py:153-171) then drops models whose id contains content-safety/guard/moderation/embed/rerank and requires output_modalities to equal exactly ['text'] -- the comment names the real reason: Lyria advertises ['text','audio'] and is an audio generator, so a 'text is present' check would wave a music model through and waste a refutation on it; a record with no declared modality is kept, because a missing field is not evidence of a missing capability. chat() (client.py:197-255) calls quota.guard() and quota.pace(3.0) BEFORE each attempt (client.py:216-217), walks a preference-ordered candidate pool (client.py:67, 174-187), retries the next zero-priced sibling only on statuses 0/429/502/503/504/524 (client.py:190-194) since any other 4xx means the request itself is wrong, logs every attempt to state/api-usage.jsonl with counted=False for transport failures and 429s (client.py:227-233), and returns the model that actually answered together with `tried`, the list of ones that did not -- kept because 'a silent substitution would make a refutation impossible to reproduce' (client.py:203-206, 239-245). _http() returns status 0 for a URLError specifically to keep 'no network' distinguishable from 'provider said no' (client.py:91-94). cmd_refute() (client.py:291-334) sends REFUTE_SYSTEM, an adversarial-verifier prompt demanding a JSON object with refuted/confidence/why/cheapest_check/assumption_found and instructing the model to default to refuted=true when evidence does not establish the claim (client.py:258-273); it accepts --claim or --claim-file (the file path exists because a long claim does not survive shell quoting and a claim whose wording mentions credentials trips the shell guard -- client.py:292-296, an explicit choice to keep the command line boring rather than reword to slip past a check), pulls the verdict out of a possibly-fenced reply (extract_json, client.py:276-288), prints failed_over_from when a substitution happened, and turns the verdict into an exit code: 1 refuted, 0 supported, 2 unparseable-reply-is-not-a-pass, and 3 from main() when the daily quota is exhausted (client.py:330-334, 455-457). cmd_selftest (client.py:388-411) is a five-step end-to-end check spending one real free call. tools/review/panel.py:554-581 is the one in-repo consumer of chat() outside the CLI.
strongest_counterargument: The split I am recommending trades a property for line count, and the property is the one the file was built to protect. `openrouter/free` picks at random. A refutation channel whose whole justification is 'a different vendor's weights, reachable over plain HTTPS' (client.py:8-10) becomes, under the router, a channel where you cannot say which weights refuted your claim before the call and cannot reproduce the choice after it -- and OpenRouter returns one final model id, so the `tried` trail that cmd_refute prints as failed_over_from is gone. The docstring calls that trail load-bearing in as many words. Deleting ~80 lines to acquire a reproducibility hole in the one tool that exists to make claims checkable is a bad trade on its own terms, and the record above admits it never actually called `openrouter/free`, never confirmed it is zero-priced, and never confirmed its 'feature filtering' excludes the audio models that _text_capable was written for after somebody presumably hit exactly that -- so the adopt half of this verdict rests on a marketing sentence on a product page, which is precisely the standard of evidence this repo refuses everywhere else. There is a second, blunter counterargument: this file is 461 lines of stdlib with zero third-party dependencies, and every alternative named here costs at least one pip install, some cost a server and a database. A one-maintainer offline-capable repo pays a real recurring price for each dependency and gets, in exchange, features this tool does not use -- streaming, tool calling, embeddings, 100 providers it will never call. Judged that way the honest verdict is keep-ours and the correct action is a two-line comment on client.py:174 saying 'openrouter/free now does this server-side; kept for reproducible model choice'. I am calling it split anyway because the failover loop, pick_model and PREFERRED are genuinely commodity now in a way they were not when this was written on 2026-07-25, and letting that go unrecorded is how a component's justification quietly ages into a story. But a future session should read this verdict as 'the routing half is no longer novel', NOT as 'rip it out' -- and should run recheck step 1 before touching a line, because if `openrouter/free` is absent or non-zero-priced the adopt half evaporates entirely.
